name: Medial epicanthoplasty

card.summary: Surgery that releases or removes the inner-corner eyelid fold to open the eye; well described in the Asian blepharoplasty literature, mostly as case series.
card.note: Scarring at the inner corner is the main reported drawback; often combined with double eyelid surgery.

quick.overview:
Medial epicanthoplasty is a plastic-surgery procedure that modifies the epicanthal fold, the skin fold covering the inner corner of the eye. The fold is common in East Asian populations, and surgeons describe the operation as widening the visible inner eye and often performing it with double-eyelid surgery.

On looksmax.org, users have discussed it as a way to change inner-corner shape and perceived eye spacing, including planning surgery in Korea. Evidence consists of surgical case series and a few small trials.
quick.mechanism: Several techniques exist, including Z-plasty, Y-V advancement and skin-redraping methods, each rearranging skin at the medial canthus to release the fold and lengthen the horizontal opening of the eye.
quick.risks: The central concern in the literature is scarring at the inner corner; a randomised split-face trial tested botulinum toxin to reduce hypertrophic scars after the operation. Other reported issues include recurrence and asymmetry.

lead: Medial epicanthoplasty is a cosmetic and reconstructive operation that reduces or removes the epicanthal fold, a vertical skin fold that partially covers the inner corner of the eye. The fold is particularly common in East Asian populations, where the epicanthal fold is described as frequently coexisting with a missing upper eyelid crease.[1][11]

Epicanthoplasty is reported mainly in the context of Asian blepharoplasty, where it is frequently combined with creation of a double eyelid fold. Surgeons in published series describe the aim as exposing more of the medial canthus and lengthening the eye's horizontal dimension.[1][2][5]

Many techniques have been published (Z-plasty and variants, Y-V advancement, skin redraping, root Z-epicanthoplasty). Reported evidence consists of retrospective series, an anatomical study and small trials, and scarring is the recurring concern.[2][3][4][6]

paras: The epicanthal fold is classified into types by origin; the Wikipedia article on the fold lists supraciliaris, palpebralis, tarsalis and inversus forms, and describes tarsalis as the type most often seen in East Asians.[11] A 475-patient Korean American series described type 2 and type 3 folds as present in the majority of the East Asian population.[3]
An anatomical and histological study examined the structure of the fold.[9] Some surgeons have argued that technique selection should depend on anatomical variation.[8]

Z-epicanthoplasty and its modifications are among the best-known approaches.[1][3][5] The Y-V advancement technique was reported in 148 cases from 1989 to 1997,[4] and a skin-redraping method was reported in a series from 2002 to 2004 with the aim of lessening scarring and design complexity.[2] A comparison of three epicanthoplasty types has also been published,[12] and combined epicanthoplasty with double eyelid surgery has been described for Chinese eyelids.[7][10]

Authors repeatedly describe scarring at the medial canthus as an obstacle to be overcome.[2][4] A split-face, double-blind randomised trial reported that early postoperative botulinum toxin type A was used to prevent hypertrophic scarring after epicanthoplasty.[6] Grokipedia, an AI-generated reference, lists scarring, under- or over-correction, asymmetry and recurrence as risks, though it should be treated with caution.[13]

Surgeons writing in the 1990s described the epicanthal fold as an element of traditional Asian beauty that many patients nonetheless sought to reduce, particularly when combined with a double-eyelid procedure.[1] Grokipedia also notes debate over whether such surgery reflects Western ideals.[13]

On looksmax.org, one user of Chinese/Kazakh background described having 'mongolic folds' and a perceived 5 to 6 mm deficit in ideal eye distance, and asked about having epicanthoplasty in South Korea, how to conceal post-operative marks, and budget.[14] The post illustrates the way the procedure is discussed as a means of altering inner-eye spacing.

Evidence includes retrospective surgical series of Z-plasty variants, Y-V advancement and skin redraping,[1][2][3][4][5] and a split-face, double-blind randomised trial of botulinum toxin for scar prevention.[6] Registered trials include a completed 14-participant study of epicanthoplasty and upper-eyelid appearance (NCT06363422)[15] and a Phase 3 botulinum toxin study with 42 participants (NCT03294382).[16]

timeline.event: Z-epicanthoplasty in Asian eyelids is published.[1]
Modified Y-V advancement epicanthoplasty is reported.[4]
A skin-redraping medial epicanthoplasty is described.[2]
An anatomical and histological study of the epicanthal fold is published.[9]
A split-face randomised trial reports botulinum toxin for scar prevention after epicanthoplasty.[6]

lore.intro: Forum discussion is sparse; a looksmax.org thread shows epicanthoplasty being weighed as a way to change inner-corner shape and eye spacing, alongside travel and recovery logistics.[14]

claims.claim: Epicanthoplasty can correct a narrow-looking eye spacing caused by 'mongolic folds'.
claims.believers: A poster says a 5-6 mm shortfall in ideal eye distance is 'mainly caused by' the folds and plans surgery in Korea for that reason.[14]
claims.experts: Surgical papers describe the operation as widening the exposed inner eye and lengthening the horizontal aperture, but report mainly surgeon-assessed outcomes in series.[1][2]

claims.claim: Post-surgical marks can be hidden with makeup within a few weeks.
claims.believers: The same poster asks whether marks could be covered after 2-3 weeks to avoid notice from family.[14]
claims.experts: Published work identifies medial canthal scarring as a persistent concern and has tested botulinum toxin to reduce hypertrophic scarring.[2][6]
